title: Piano Sonata No. 32 in C minor
hook: Beethoven’s last piano sonata: a short storm, then a long, slow song that slowly lifts away.

painting.title: The Voyage of Life: Old Age
painting.pairingNote: An old man’s boat has come through the storm to still, dark water, and a light opens above him; the sonata makes the same journey, from a C minor storm to a slow song that seems to rise beyond it.

facts: Beethoven wrote it in 1821–22, aged fifty-one. It is the last of his thirty-two piano sonatas and the last of three he planned together (Opp. 109, 110 and 111). He dedicated it to his pupil and patron Archduke Rudolf.

It has only two movements: a stormy Allegro in C minor and a long, slow set of [[variation|variation]]s in C major. His secretary Anton Schindler, an unreliable witness, claimed that Beethoven, asked why there was no third movement, answered that he had not had time. The sketches suggest he dropped the idea of a third movement himself.
Contemporaries largely ignored it. Leading pianists took it up only in the second half of the 19th century.
In Thomas Mann’s novel *Doctor Faustus* a music teacher gives a whole lecture on why Op. 111 needs no third movement: after this ending, he says, there could be no return.
bigPicture.inOneLine: struggle (I), and a slow song that is varied until it seems to dissolve into light (II).

movements.heading: Maestoso – Allegro con brio ed appassionato
movements.tempo: Maestoso – Allegro con brio ed appassionato
movements.summary: A slow, grim introduction of hammered chords and wide leaps, then a fierce, fast movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], driven by a short, angry theme that keeps turning into counterpoint. At the very end the storm dies away into a quiet C major chord.

mainIdeas.name: The Maestoso
mainIdeas.description: loud, harsh chords in a jagged dotted rhythm, with the left hand leaping a long way down; then low trills rumbling in the bass.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a short, fierce figure, first in bare octaves low in the bass, then piled up in several voices like a [[fugue|fugue]].

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: brief and gentle, in A-flat major; the music slows almost to a stop.

stops.hear: Loud, jagged chords, with a wide leap down in the left hand; long silences between them
A low, rumbling trill in the bass that grows
Fast and fierce: a short, angry figure in bare octaves, low in the bass, then in both hands
Softer and gentler for a moment; the music slows almost to a stop
The angry figure from the start of the Allegro again
The figure enters in one hand, then the other, piling up
The angry figure in full force, back in C minor

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The storm drains away; soft rising and falling figures, and a quiet C major chord
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]], turning from minor to major

notice: Listen to how short the gentle second theme is. It barely gets started before the storm takes over again.
The last chord is major, and quiet. It already points to the second movement.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Kempff takes the repeat of the exposition (≈ 3:45). From the track length this looks certain, but it has not been checked by ear.

movements.heading: Arietta. Adagio molto semplice e cantabile
movements.tempo: Arietta. Adagio molto semplice e cantabile
movements.summary: A slow, simple tune (“arietta” means little song), then a chain of [[variation|variation]]s. The beat stays the same throughout, but the notes get faster in each variation, until the music becomes rhythmic, almost dance-like. Then it turns quiet, rises to the top of the keyboard, and ends in a long, shimmering haze of [[trill|trill]]s.

mainIdeas.name: The Arietta
mainIdeas.description: a slow, calm melody in C major, in short phrases, each half played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The quickening
mainIdeas.description: in each of the first three variations the notes are subdivided further, so the same pulse feels faster and more excited.

mainIdeas.name: The trills
mainIdeas.description: long, held trills that make the high notes shimmer, as if the sound were suspended.

stops.hear: A slow, calm tune in the middle of the keyboard, in simple chords
The same tune, now with a gentle, flowing rhythm underneath
Livelier, with a lilting dotted rhythm
Loud and fast: jagged, swinging rhythms that tumble down the keyboard
stops.happening: Variation 3. Many listeners hear something like jazz or boogie-woogie in it

stops.hear: Suddenly very soft: a dark murmur low in the bass, then the same idea high and glittering
A chain of long trills; the music seems to stop moving forward
stops.happening: A free passage, out of the variations

stops.hear: Quiet; the tune’s first notes come back, hesitantly, in a far-off key
stops.happening: The theme looks for its way home

stops.hear: The tune returns in C major, whole, with a flowing accompaniment
A trill held high above the tune; everything thins out

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The opening notes of the tune, a last swell, and a quiet final chord

notice: Tap the slow beat at the start and keep tapping. In variation 3 the beat is the same; only the notes inside it have become faster.
In the coda, listen to the right hand. One finger sustains a trill while others still play the melody.

threads.title: Two worlds
threads.body: Minor and major, fast and slow, struggle and calm: the two movements are as opposite as Beethoven could make them.

threads.title: The whole keyboard
threads.body: The first movement digs into the lowest notes of the piano; the second ends at its very top.

threads.title: Counting time
threads.body: The theme’s slow pulse never changes, yet the music speeds up and slows down by changing how finely each beat is divided.

threads.title: The last sonata
threads.body: After Op. 111 Beethoven wrote more piano music, the Diabelli Variations and the Bagatelles, but never another piano sonata.
